plan: Informative essay (CLD-P-ACT-E-000049) on the zipper: Judson's 1893 clasp locker patent, Sundback's interlocking teeth, the hookless fastener name, and the B. F. Goodrich boots (naming story hedged as 'is said to'). Topic checked against every bank (no matches). Eight items, three aimed at hard (fragment with a relative clause, dangling modifier with two tempting variants, essay purpose with a true-but-partial distractor). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: A Better Way to Fasten Boots
passages.text:
[1] In 1893, an inventor named Whitcomb Judson patented a device he called a "clasp locker." [2] It was meant to replace the long rows of buttons and hooks on high boots, {{1|but it had a serious flaw: it}} tended to pop open without warning.

[3] The problem was solved two decades later by Gideon Sundback, a Swedish-born engineer working for the company that had acquired Judson's patents. [4] {{2|Sundback's design, which used}} rows of small interlocking teeth, each shaped with a tiny hook on one side and a hollow on the other. [5] A slider pressed the teeth together so that each hook nested inside the hollow of the tooth across from it. [6] {{4|Increasing the number of teeth per inch, the fastener became both smaller and far more secure.}}

[7] Sundback called his invention the "hookless fastener," a name that {{5|did little to excite}} customers. [8] The device did not catch on until 1923, when the B. F. Goodrich Company used it on a line of rubber boots. {{10|}} [9] The company's president is said to have enjoyed the sound the boots made as they were closed{{6| and he decided to call}} them "Zippers." [10] Before long, the name had spread from the boots to the fastener itself.

[11] Today, zippers close everything from jackets to tents to suitcases. [12] {{8|Few of the people who use them every day knows}} that the device began as a better way to fasten boots.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: but it had a serious flaw, it
choices.C: but it had a serious flaw it
choices.D: but it had a serious flaw, which it

candidates.evidence: tended to pop open without warning
candidates.explanation: The colon follows a complete clause and introduces an explanation of the flaw.

B.rationale: A comma alone joins two independent clauses, creating a comma splice.

C.rationale: Without punctuation, two independent clauses run together.

D.rationale: "Which it tended to pop open" is not a grammatical clause.

hints: Is "it tended to pop open without warning" a complete sentence?

strategy.explanation: Check how the explanation is attached.

candidates.remember: A colon after a complete clause can introduce an explanation.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.explanation: The subject "Sundback's design" needs a main verb. "Sundback's design used rows of small interlocking teeth" is a complete sentence.

A.rationale: "Which used" turns the rest into a clause describing the design, leaving the sentence without a main verb.

B.rationale: "Using" is not a main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

C.rationale: "That used" also makes a describing clause, so the sentence still has no main verb.

hints: Does sentence 4 have a main verb?

strategy.explanation: Find the subject and look for its verb.

candidates.remember: A relative clause cannot supply a sentence's main verb.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Having increased the number of teeth per inch, the fastener became both smaller and far more secure.
choices.C: By increasing the number of teeth per inch, Sundback made the fastener both smaller and far more secure.
choices.D: Increasing the number of teeth per inch, smaller and far more secure was what the fastener became.

candidates.explanation: Only C names the person who increased the number of teeth, Sundback, so the introductory phrase has a logical subject.

A.rationale: The fastener did not increase the number of teeth; the modifier dangles.

B.rationale: The fastener still appears to be the one that increased the teeth.

D.rationale: The modifier still has no logical subject, and the word order is awkward.

hints: Who increased the number of teeth?

strategy.explanation: Make sure that person follows the introductory phrase.

candidates.remember: An introductory modifier must describe the noun right after the comma.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: did little to thrill and excite

candidates.explanation: "Did little to excite" says concisely that the name failed to interest customers, which sets up the next sentence.

C.rationale: "A little" reverses the meaning, suggesting the name helped somewhat.

hints: What does the next sentence say about sales?

strategy.explanation: Check each choice for meaning and wordiness.

candidates.remember: "Little" and "a little" mean nearly opposite things.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
candidates.evidence: enjoyed the sound the boots made
candidates.explanation: The president enjoyed the sound, so he named the boots after it: ", so" joins the clauses and shows cause and effect.

A.rationale: Two independent clauses joined by "and" need a comma, and "and" also hides the cause-and-effect relationship.

C.rationale: , although" signals a contrast, but enjoying the sound is the reason for the name.

D.rationale: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, not a phrase.

hints: Why did the president call the boots "Zippers"?

strategy.explanation: Identify the relationship between the two clauses.

candidates.remember: Use "so" to show that one action caused another.

candidates.stem: Which choice is best for the underlined portion?

choices.B: Few of the people who use them every day has known
choices.C: Few of the people who use them every day know
choices.D: Few of the people who use them every day is knowing

candidates.explanation: "Few" is plural, so its verb must be plural: "Few ... know."

A.rationale: The subject "Few" is plural, so "knows" does not agree with it.

B.rationale: "Has" is singular and does not agree with "Few."

D.rationale: "Is" is singular, and the progressive form is not idiomatic here.

hints: What is the subject of the verb?

strategy.explanation: Cross out "of the people who use them every day."

candidates.subskill: Evaluating whether an essay meets a goal
candidates.stem: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to explain how a product came to have its name. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains that a company president named a line of boots after the sound they made.
choices.B: Yes, because it describes in detail the interlocking teeth that made the fastener secure.
choices.C: No, because it never explains where the word "zipper" came from in the first place.
choices.D: No, because although it explains the name's origin, it focuses mainly on developing the fastener.

candidates.evidence: Before long, the name had spread from the boots to the fastener itself.
candidates.explanation: The naming story occupies only two sentences; most of the essay describes Judson's device and Sundback's design, so the essay does not have naming as its primary purpose.

A.rationale: This is true, but it is a small part of the essay, which mostly describes the invention.

B.rationale: Describing the teeth does not explain how the product got its name.

C.rationale: Sentences 9 and 10 explain where the word came from.

hints: How much of the essay is about the name?

strategy.explanation: Compare the goal with the essay's main focus, then check each reason.

candidates.remember: An essay meets a purpose only if that purpose is its main focus.

candidates.stem:
At this point, the writer is considering adding the following sentence:
Rubber boots were especially popular among farmers in rainy regions.
Should the writer make this addition here?

choices.A: Yes, because it explains why the boots with the new fastener sold so well.
choices.B: Yes, because it identifies the first people who used the new fastener.
choices.C: No, because the boots' buyers are unrelated to the history of the fastener.
choices.D: No, because it contradicts the statement that the boots were made by Goodrich.

candidates.evidence: used it on a line of rubber boots
candidates.explanation: The paragraph traces how the fastener got its name; who bought rubber boots is off topic.

A.rationale: The sentence says nothing about why the boots sold well.

B.rationale: The sentence describes rubber boots in general, not who first used the fastener.

D.rationale: The sentence does not mention who made the boots.

strategy.explanation: State its focus, then test the sentence.

candidates.remember: Add a sentence only if it supports the paragraph's focus.
